analysis.one_liner: Speeds federal permitting for energy and mining projects and mandates annual offshore oil, gas, and wind lease sales.
analysis.headline: The Senate Energy Committee favorably reported the bill on July 31, 2024 and placed it on the Senate calendar on December 19, but the full Senate never voted before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would shorten the time companies wait for federal approval of energy, mining, and transmission projects, and cut the window for lawsuits challenging those approvals to 150 days. It would require the Interior Department to hold at least one offshore oil and gas lease sale and one offshore wind lease sale every year from 2025 through 2029, and it would deem natural gas export applications approved if the Energy Department misses a deadline. It also would speed renewable energy rights-of-way, geothermal drilling, and interstate electric transmission lines, with new protections shielding customers who get no benefit from paying transmission costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Energy and mining companies get the most: faster coal lease decisions, required yearly offshore oil and gas sales, automatic approval of LNG export applications the government fails to act on, and fewer federal permit requirements when wells sit mostly on private land. Renewable developers, geothermal companies, and transmission builders also gain from deadlines, streamlined reviews, and expanded federal permitting authority. Consumers could benefit indirectly if faster transmission lines and cheaper generation lower power prices.

how_it_helps.text: Sets deadlines across the permitting system, including 90-day starts on federal coal lease reviews and 30-day decisions on renewable energy rights-of-way and geothermal drilling permits, so projects are not stuck in agency backlogs for years [S2][S3].

Requires FERC to plan transmission with neighboring regions and protects ratepayers: customers who receive no benefit, or only trivial benefit, from new transmission cannot be involuntarily charged for it [S3].
Mandates at least one offshore wind lease sale per year from 2025 to 2029, offering at least 400,000 acres annually, and sets a 30-gigawatt offshore wind production goal [S3].
Routes fees from expanded hardrock mining mill sites into an Abandoned Hardrock Mine Fund dedicated to cleaning up abandoned mines under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act [S3].
Requires reliability assessments of proposed federal regulations that could threaten grid reliability, giving states and grid operators a formal check before rules take effect [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Communities near new drilling, mining, and export terminals face shorter windows to challenge federal approvals in court and, in some cases, weaker federal oversight: wells on mostly private land in a drilling unit would no longer need a federal permit to drill, and operators could not be required to post bonds protecting non-federal land or obtain approval for surface reclamation. More public land and offshore acreage would be leased for oil, gas, and mining, with the associated pollution and climate effects. Environmental review and litigation rights, the main leverage ordinary citizens have over federal projects, are narrowed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near energy and mining projects

drawbacks.text: A civil action challenging an energy or mining authorization must be filed within 150 days or is barred, and courts must set expedited schedules, sharply shortening the time communities and conservation groups have to contest approvals [S2][S3].
Interior must hold at least one offshore oil and gas lease sale each year from 2025 through 2029 regardless of the existing 2024-2029 leasing program [S2][S3].
Liquefied natural gas export applications are deemed approved if the Energy Department misses its deadline, removing the practical ability to withhold approval [S2].

On split-estate drilling units where the federal government owns less than half the minerals and none of the surface, no federal permit to drill is required, and Interior may not require bonds to protect non-federal land, impose mitigation, or require approval for surface reclamation [S3].
Expanding FERC's authority to permit interstate transmission without a DOE corridor designation can override state and local siting decisions for power lines [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real trade at the heart of this bill. Faster transmission planning, geothermal and renewable permitting, and the ratepayer-protection language would address genuine grid problems that raise costs for everyone. But those gains are bought with weaker environmental review, a much shorter window for citizens to sue, required annual offshore oil and gas sales, and automatic approval of gas export applications, all of which favor extraction industries. Whether the package is good for the public depends on weighing cheaper, more reliable power against expanded fossil development on public lands and offshore waters with reduced public oversight.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Energy Committee approved it and put it on the Senate's calendar in mid-December 2024, but the Congress ended January 3, 2025 without the full Senate ever voting on it.

narrative.text: Sen. Joe Manchin, an independent from West Virginia, introduced the bill on July 23, 2024 for himself and Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming, the top Republican on the Energy Committee; it was one Republican cosponsor [S3][S4][S5].
The Committee on Energy and Natural Resources ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment on July 31, 2024, and formally reported it on December 19, 2024 with Report 118-336 [S5].

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 756) on December 19, 2024, a step that makes it ready for floor consideration but does not guarantee a vote [S5].
No floor vote ever occurred; the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still on the calendar, so every provision lapsed [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Status quo: energy and mining companies keep operating under today's slower, more contestable permitting rules, while communities retain full environmental-review and litigation rights, and the existing limits on offshore drilling and LNG export approvals remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies under current permitting rules and nearby communities

industries.note: The bill mandates at least one offshore oil and gas lease sale per year from 2025 to 2029, speeds drilling permits, refunds nomination fees, and exempts split-estate wells from federal drilling permits, bonds, mitigation, and reclamation approval. These changes expand access to public and offshore resources while cutting the oversight tools nearby residents and the public rely on.

DOE would face a deadline to approve or deny export applications, with missed deadlines counting as automatic approval, effectively guaranteeing permits. More exports can raise domestic natural gas prices while opening lucrative foreign markets for producers.

The bill sets hard deadlines for commencing coal lease reviews, issuing records of decision, and setting fair market value within 30 days, making it harder for administrations to slow or decline federal coal leasing. Coal lease terms like reasonable foreseeable development planning remain, but the clock now favors applicants.

Mining claim holders can locate unlimited 5-acre mill sites for waste rock and tailings under approved plans of operations, with claim maintenance fees routed to an abandoned mine cleanup fund. This expands industry use of public land while creating a dedicated cleanup funding stream, though it does not modernize the 1872 royalty-free claim system.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and offshore wind developers
industries.note: Deadlines for rights-of-way decisions, categorical exclusions for low-disturbance activities, a 50 GW renewable goal on federal land, and mandated annual offshore wind lease sales of at least 400,000 acres would speed clean energy projects that also serve public decarbonization and lower energy costs.

Annual leasing instead of every two years, 30-day drilling permit decisions, categorical exclusions for exploration, and a federal ombudsman would substantially speed geothermal projects, a low-emission power source.

FERC gains authority to permit interstate transmission lines in the national interest without a DOE corridor designation, and regions must jointly plan interregional lines, easing the biggest bottleneck to cheap clean power. But ratepayer-protection clauses bar charging customers who receive no benefit, and state siting authority is partly preempted.
